DOMESTIC VIOLENCE CUSTODY PRESUMPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Riley Lee · Jordan Alex Lee

DECLARATION REGARDING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE CUSTODY PRESUMPTION INFORMATION
This information sheet concerns a child custody proceeding involving Riley Lee, filed or to be filed in Sacramento County County, California, between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee. It is prepared to explain California Family Code section 3044 -- the statute that creates a rebuttable presumption against awarding sole or joint custody to a parent whom a court has found to have perpetrated domestic violence within a specified look-back period, and that lists the factors a court considers in deciding whether that presumption has been overcome. This information sheet is a companion to, and distinct from, this corpus's Domestic Violence Restraining Order Information Sheet: that document explains the process for obtaining a protective order under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Family Code section 6200 et seq.); this document explains a separate, later-stage legal consequence -- how a court finding of domestic violence affects a subsequent custody determination under Family Code section 3044. This information sheet does not itself assert that either party has perpetrated domestic violence, does not assert that the presumption applies to this matter, and does not make or substitute for any finding a court is required to make under Family Code section 3044 -- only the court, applying section 3044 to the evidence and facts of the case before it, can make that determination.

THE CORE REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION -- FAMILY CODE SECTION 3044(A)
Family Code section 3044(a) provides that upon a finding by the court that a party seeking custody of a child has perpetrated domestic violence within the previous five years against the other party seeking custody of the child, or against the child or the child's siblings, or against a person described in Family Code section 3011(a)(2)(A) with whom the party has a relationship, there is a rebuttable presumption that an award of sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to a person who has perpetrated domestic violence is detrimental to the best interest of the child. The persons described in Family Code section 3011(a)(2)(A) are: a child to whom the parent or person seeking custody is related by blood or affinity or with whom that parent or person has had a caretaking relationship, no matter how temporary; the other parent; and a parent, current spouse, or cohabitant of the parent or person seeking custody, or a person with whom that parent or person has a dating or engagement relationship. The statute states that this presumption may only be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon a finding by the court that a party seeking custody of a child has perpetrated domestic violence within the previous five years against the other party seeking custody of the child, or against the child or the child’s siblings, or against a person in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3011 with whom the party has a relationship, there is a rebuttable presumption that an award of sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to a person who has perpetrated domestic violence is detrimental to the best interest of the child, pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. This presumption may only be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(a), the core rebuttable presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "(2) (A) A history of abuse by one parent or any other person seeking custody against any of the following: (i) A child to whom the parent or person seeking custody is related by blood or affinity or with whom the parent or person seeking custody has had a caretaking relationship, no matter how temporary. (ii) The other parent. (iii) A parent, current spouse, or cohabitant, of the parent or person seeking custody, or a person with whom the parent or person seeking custody has a dating or engagement relationship."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a)(2)(A), the persons protected by the presumption, as cross-referenced by section 3044(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3011.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two different, independently numbered Family Code sections -- section 3044(a) and section 3011(a)(2)(A), which section 3044(a) itself cross-references by citation -- rather than two subsections of the same section, so this is not a case requiring the single-section-independence disclosure; however, because section 3044(a) incorporates section 3011(a)(2)(A) by direct cross-reference rather than restating it, the two quotes together describe one integrated statutory rule, not two separately corroborating sources on the same point. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own custody-presumption rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter, and not a claim that an equivalent presumption exists in every state (domestic-violence-related custody presumptions vary significantly by state, including whether one exists at all, the look-back period, and what conduct or relationships trigger it). The version of section 3044 quoted throughout this document was added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544 (SB 899) and became operative January 1, 2026; this research fetched and confirmed that current, operative text directly (twice, from independent requests) rather than relying on a summary or an earlier version of the section. Whether a specific party's conduct meets the threshold for a court "finding" that domestic violence was "perpetrated," and whether a specific relationship falls within section 3011(a)(2)(A), are determinations the court makes on the evidence before it -- this clause states only the statutory text, not how it applies to any individual's facts.

OVERCOMING THE PRESUMPTION -- THE STATUTORY FACTORS UNDER SECTION 3044(B)
Family Code section 3044(b) states that to overcome the presumption in subdivision (a), the court shall find that paragraph (1) is satisfied and shall find that the factors in paragraph (2), on balance, support the legislative findings in Family Code section 3020. Paragraph (1) requires that the perpetrator of domestic violence has demonstrated that giving sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to the perpetrator is in the best interest of the child under Family Code sections 3011 and 3020, and specifies that in making that determination, the preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents (Family Code section 3020(b)) or with the noncustodial parent (Family Code section 3040(a)(1)) may not be used to rebut the presumption, in whole or in part. Paragraph (2) lists these additional factors: (A) whether the perpetrator has successfully completed a batterer's treatment program meeting the criteria in Penal Code section 1203.097(c); (B) whether the perpetrator has successfully completed a program of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, if the court determines counseling is appropriate; (C) whether the perpetrator has successfully completed a parenting class, if the court determines the class is appropriate; (D) whether the perpetrator is on probation or parole, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions; (E) whether the perpetrator is restrained by a protective order or restraining order, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions; (F) whether the perpetrator has committed further acts of domestic violence; and (G) whether the court has determined, under Family Code section 6322.5, that the perpetrator is a restrained person in possession or control of a firearm or ammunition in violation of Family Code section 6389, Code of Civil Procedure section 527.9, or Penal Code section 18120.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The perpetrator of domestic violence has demonstrated that giving sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to the perpetrator is in the best interest of the child pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. In determining the best interest of the child, the preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents, as set forth in subdivision (b) of Section 3020, or with the noncustodial parent, as set forth in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3040, may not be used to rebut the presumption, in whole or in part."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(b)(1), the best-interest showing required, and the bar on using the frequent-contact preference to rebut (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "(A) The perpetrator has successfully completed a batterer’s treatment program that meets the criteria outlined in subdivision (c) of Section 1203.097 of the Penal Code. (B) The perpetrator has successfully completed a program of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, if the court determines that counseling is appropriate. (C) The perpetrator has successfully completed a parenting class, if the court determines the class to be appropriate. (D) The perpetrator is on probation or parole, and has or has not complied with the terms and conditions of probation or parole. (E) The perpetrator is restrained by a protective order or restraining order, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions. (F) The perpetrator of domestic violence has committed further acts of domestic violence. (G) The court has determined, pursuant to Section 6322.5, that the perpetrator is a restrained person in possession or control of a firearm or ammunition in violation of Section 6389, Section 527.9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Section 18120 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(b)(2)(A)-(G), the seven additional rebuttal factors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 3044(b), including its paragraph (1) and the seven lettered factors of paragraph (2), are all provisions of a single statutory section (§ 3044); no additional, independently-numbered statutory source exists for this specific factor list, so this clause relies on a single section for its core content, though the cross-referenced provisions it names (sections 3020, 3040, 1203.097 of the Penal Code, 6322.5, 6389, and Code of Civil Procedure section 527.9) are each independently enacted and are quoted as section 3044(b) itself frames them, not independently re-verified against their own full text in this research pass. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific factor list California's presumption directs a court to weigh -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter, and other states' domestic-violence custody presumptions, where they exist, commonly use different rebuttal factors. This clause states the statutory list only; it does not state whether any specific party has satisfied any of these factors, and does not state how a court weighs the factors relative to one another beyond the statute's own "on balance" language.

HOW "PERPETRATED DOMESTIC VIOLENCE" IS ESTABLISHED FOR THIS SECTION
Family Code section 3044(c) provides its own, self-contained definition of when a person has "perpetrated domestic violence" for purposes of this section: when the person is found by the court to have intentionally or recklessly caused or attempted to cause bodily injury, or sexual assault, or to have placed a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another, or to have engaged in behavior involving, but not limited to, threatening, striking, harassing, destroying personal property, or disturbing the peace of another, for which a court may issue an ex parte order under Family Code section 6320. Separately, Family Code section 3044(d)(1) states that the required court finding may also be satisfied by evidence that a party has been convicted, within the previous five years, after a trial or a plea of guilty or no contest, of a crime against the other party that comes within the definition of domestic violence contained in Family Code section 6211 and of abuse contained in Family Code section 6203. Section 3044(d)(2) states that the finding requirement is also satisfied if any court -- whether or not it is hearing the custody proceeding -- has made a finding under subdivision (a) based on conduct occurring within the previous five years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For purposes of this section, a person has “perpetrated domestic violence” when the person is found by the court to have intentionally or recklessly caused or attempted to cause bodily injury, or sexual assault, or to have placed a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another, or to have engaged in behavior involving, but not limited to, threatening, striking, harassing, destroying personal property, or disturbing the peace of another, for which a court may issue an ex parte order pursuant to Section 6320 to protect the other party seeking custody of the child or to protect the child and the child’s siblings."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(c), the self-contained definition of "perpetrated domestic violence" for this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "For purposes of this section, the requirement of a finding by the court shall be satisfied by, among other things, and not limited to, evidence that a party seeking custody has been convicted within the previous five years, after a trial or a plea of guilty or no contest, of a crime against the other party that comes within the definition of domestic violence contained in Section 6211 and of abuse contained in Section 6203, including, but not limited to, a crime described in subdivision (e) of Section 243 of, or Section 261, 273.5, 422, or 646.9 of, or former Section 262 of, the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(d)(1), how the required court finding may be established by prior conviction referencing sections 6211 and 6203 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "The requirement of a finding by the court shall also be satisfied if a court, whether that court hears or has heard the child custody proceedings or not, has made a finding pursuant to subdivision (a) based on conduct occurring within the previous five years."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(d)(2), the finding requirement is also satisfied by another court's prior finding under subdivision (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same statutory section (§ 3044); the cross-referenced sections 6211 and 6203 are independently-numbered Family Code sections, but this research did not independently re-fetch and quote their full current text in this document (section 6211's current text was separately spot-checked, without a formal two-fetch confirmation, and found consistent with the definition already verified and cited in this corpus's DVRO Petition Information document, but is not independently cited here). The important, easily-missed nuance this clause is built around: section 3044 does not simply cross-reference the DVPA's "domestic violence" definition (§ 6211) or "abuse" definition (§ 6203) as the general test for whether this section's presumption applies -- subdivision (c) sets out its own definition of "perpetrated domestic violence," which overlaps substantially with, but is not textually identical to, section 6203's abuse definition (both include causing or attempting bodily injury, sexual assault, and placing a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury; the DVPA cross-reference to sections 6211 and 6203 appears only in subdivision (d)(1), as one specific way -- a prior criminal conviction -- of satisfying the finding requirement, not as the operative definition for a contested finding made directly under subdivision (a). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California structures this specific definitional question -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that other states structure an analogous presumption's triggering definition the same way.

WHEN AND HOW THE FINDING IS MADE -- INTERACTION WITH THE GENERAL CUSTODY PROCESS
Family Code section 3044(g) states that in an evidentiary hearing or trial in which custody orders are sought and where there has been an allegation of domestic violence, the court shall determine whether this section applies before issuing a custody order, unless the court finds a continuance necessary to make that determination -- in which case the court may issue a temporary custody order for a reasonable period, provided the order complies with Family Code sections 3011 and 3020. Section 3044(e) states that when a court makes a finding that a party has perpetrated domestic violence, the court may not base that finding solely on conclusions reached by a child custody evaluator or on the recommendation of Family Court Services staff, but shall consider any relevant, admissible evidence submitted by the parties. Section 3044(f)(1) states that it is the intent of the Legislature that subdivision (f) be interpreted consistently with Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, which requires the court, in determining that the presumption has been overcome, to make specific findings on each of the factors in subdivision (b); section 3044(f)(2) requires the court, if it determines the presumption has been overcome, to state its reasons in writing or on the record for why subdivision (b)'s paragraph (1) is satisfied and why the paragraph (2) factors, on balance, support the legislative findings in section 3020. Section 3044(h) separately requires that in a custody or restraining order proceeding where a party has alleged the other party perpetrated domestic violence under this section, the court shall inform the parties of the existence of this section and give them a copy of it before custody mediation in the case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In an evidentiary hearing or trial in which custody orders are sought and where there has been an allegation of domestic violence, the court shall make a determination as to whether this section applies prior to issuing a custody order, unless the court finds that a continuance is necessary to determine whether this section applies, in which case the court may issue a temporary custody order for a reasonable period of time, provided the order complies with Sections 3011 and 3020."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(g), the requirement to determine applicability before a custody order issues, and the temporary-order exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature that this subdivision be interpreted consistently with the decision in Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, which requires that the court, in determining that the presumption in subdivision (a) has been overcome, make specific findings on each of the factors in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(f)(1), the Jaime G. v. H.L. specific-findings requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "If the court determines that the presumption in subdivision (a) has been overcome, the court shall state its reasons in writing or on the record as to why paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) is satisfied and why the factors in paragraph (2) of subdivision (b), on balance, support the legislative findings in Section 3020."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(f)(2), the written-reasons requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  Known gap: Subdivisions (e), (f), (g), and (h) are all provisions of a single statutory section (§ 3044); this clause does not draw on a second, independent statutory source, though it does cite one case, Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, only because the statute's own text names that decision and directs that subdivision (f) be interpreted consistently with it -- this clause states what the statute says about that case, not an independent reading of the opinion itself, which was not separately retrieved or reviewed for this clause. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own procedural sequencing and evidentiary rules for this specific presumption -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding. This clause does not restate Family Code section 3011's full best-interest factor list or Family Code section 3020's legislative findings referenced throughout section 3044(b) and (g); those are separate statutory provisions this document does not independently verify or reproduce.

REQUIRED NOTICE TO THE PARTIES BEFORE CUSTODY MEDIATION
Family Code section 3044(h) provides that in a custody or restraining order proceeding in which a party has alleged that the other party has perpetrated domestic violence in accordance with the terms of this section, the court shall inform the parties of the existence of this section and shall give them a copy of this section before custody mediation in the case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In a custody or restraining order proceeding in which a party has alleged that the other party has perpetrated domestic violence in accordance with the terms of this section, the court shall inform the parties of the existence of this section and shall give them a copy of this section prior to custody mediation in the case."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(h), the requirement to inform parties of this section and provide a copy before custody mediation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  Known gap: This is a single provision of Family Code section 3044 (subdivision (h)); no independent second source was sought for this specific procedural requirement, which is stated plainly and only once in the statute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, checkable procedural step California's own courts must take -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding, and not a claim that an equivalent notice-before-mediation requirement exists in every state's custody mediation process. This clause states only that the statute requires this notice; it does not describe California's broader custody mediation process itself, which this document does not otherwise cover.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT -- NOT A COURT FINDING
I, Jordan Alex Lee, acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet regarding California Family Code section 3044 in connection with the custody proceeding concerning Riley Lee.

Executed on September 1, 2026, at Oakland, California.

☐ _________________________ Jordan Alex Lee, signature

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing in the appropriate California superior court. It does not itself find that any party has perpetrated domestic violence, does not itself apply or rebut the presumption described in this document, and does not modify any existing custody order concerning Riley Lee. Only a court, applying Family Code section 3044 to the specific facts and evidence presented to it, can make the findings this section describes.]

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 3044(g) states that in an evidentiary hearing or trial in which custody orders are sought and where there has been an allegation of domestic violence, the court shall determine whether this section applies before issuing a custody order, unless the court finds a continuance necessary to make that determination -- in which case the court may issue a temporary custody order for a reasonable period, provided the order complies with Family Code sections 3011 and 3020. Section 3044(e) states that when a court makes a finding that a party has perpetrated domestic violence, the court may not base that finding solely on conclusions reached by a child custody evaluator or on the recommendation of Family Court Services staff, but shall consider any relevant, admissible evidence submitted by the parties. Section 3044(f)(1) states that it is the intent of the Legislature that subdivision (f) be interpreted consistently with Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, which requires the court, in determining that the presumption has been overcome, to make specific findings on each of the factors in subdivision (b); section 3044(f)(2) requires the court, if it determines the presumption has been overcome, to state its reasons in writing or on the record for why subdivision (b)'s paragraph (1) is satisfied and why the paragraph (2) factors, on balance, support the legislative findings in section 3020. Section 3044(h) separately requires that in a custody or restraining order proceeding where a party has alleged the other party perpetrated domestic violence under this section, the court shall inform the parties of the existence of this section and give them a copy of it before custody mediation in the case.
